name.text: WAT 21.1: The Block That Cleans Itself!

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write three functions that drive a supplied valve through a with statement.

How this works in Python

Java shuts a resource for you with try-with-resources.

try (Valve valve = new Valve("inlet")) {
    valve.flow(5);
}

The compiler accepts that only when Valve implements AutoCloseable. On the way out of the block it calls close() for you.

Before that syntax arrived you wrote the shape by hand, and plenty of code still does.

Valve valve = new Valve("inlet");
try {
    valve.flow(5);
} finally {
    valve.close();
}

Python has one statement for both, and it is called with.

with Valve("inlet") as valve:
    valve.flow(5)

What the statement does

Three things happen, and only the middle one is yours.

with Valve("inlet") as valve:      the object is asked to open, and hands back a value
    valve.flow(5)                  your work, with no shutting anywhere in it
                                   the object is asked to shut, right here

The name after as catches whatever the opening step handed back. In this exercise that is the valve itself, which is the common case.

The object decides what leaving means

Java fixes the method name. Every AutoCloseable gets closed, and closing is all the language knows how to ask for. Python asks the object two questions instead, through a pair of dunder methods called __enter__ and __exit__. The object fills them with whatever arriving and leaving are supposed to mean for it.

For a valve that is shutting. For a transaction it is a commit or a rollback. For a lock it is a release, and for a changed setting it is putting the old value back. The block above holds none of that. It holds the work and nothing else.

There is no interface to implement either. Any object carrying the two methods can go after with. The supplied Valve class shows you both. Reading them is fine, and writing your own is the next tier.

Leaving happens either way

This is the part worth proving to yourself. The shutting step runs when the block finishes, when the block raises, and when the block hands back a value with return. Your first function returns from inside the block, and the log still records the valve shutting afterwards.

Running the cleanup is not the same as handling the failure. When the block raises, the valve shuts and the exception then carries on out to the caller. Catching it stays a separate job, and the third function does that with a try wrapped round the outside of the with.

Look at what has gone from the Python. The word finally never appears. A finally block at the call site means every caller has to remember it, and one forgetful caller leaves a valve open. with moves the remembering out of the caller and into the object, once.

Reading the log

LOG is a module-level list the supplied class writes to, so you can see the order of events without touching a file. The tests print it. Every test after the first clears it first, so each one starts from nothing.

Your task

The answer box already holds LOG and the Valve class. Leave both alone. valve.flow(litres) records the flow and hands back the number of litres.

  • pour(name, litres) drives a Valve(name) through a with block and returns what valve.flow(litres) hands back. Return from inside the block.
  • pour_many(names, litres) takes a list of names. It opens one valve per name, each in its own with block, and returns the total of every flow.
  • pour_and_fail(name) opens a valve, calls valve.flow(1), then raises ValueError("line burst") inside the block. Catch that ValueError outside the with as problem and return f"caught {problem}".

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Every function drives the valve through a with statement. A hidden test looks for the word.
  • Do not write finally anywhere. The valve shuts itself, and that is the whole point.
  • Do not call __enter__ or __exit__ by hand. The with statement calls both for you.
  • Leave the supplied Valve class and the LOG list alone.
  • Annotate every signature, parameters and return alike.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

testcode.text: LOG.clear() print(pour_many(["a", "b"], 2)) print(LOG) LOG.clear() print(pour_and_fail("outlet")) print(LOG)

expected.text: 4 ['open a', 'flow a 2', 'shut a', 'open b', 'flow b 2', 'shut b'] caught line burst ['open outlet', 'flow outlet 1', 'shut outlet']

testcode.text: import inspect for fn in (pour, pour_many, pour_and_fail): src = inspect.getsource(fn) assert "with " in src, "rule broken: every function drives the valve through a with statement" assert "finally" not in src, "rule broken: the valve shuts itself, so write no finally" assert "__enter__" not in src and "__exit__" not in src, "rule broken: let with call them for you" LOG.clear() print(pour("relay", 0)) print(pour_many([], 9)) print(LOG)

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write two context manager classes of your own, and one function that runs work inside the first.

How this works in Python

Java's try-with-resources needs AutoCloseable, and the whole interface is one method.

public interface AutoCloseable {
    void close() throws Exception;
}

close() is told nothing. It takes no arguments, so it cannot see whether the block finished or threw, it cannot record which, and it has no way to stop an exception on its way out.

Python asks for two methods and tells them everything.

class Session:
    def __enter__(self) -> list[int]:
        ...

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback) -> None:
        ...

Both are dunder methods from the dunder methods topic, so Python calls them and you never call them by name. There is no interface to implement and nothing to declare. Any object carrying the pair can go after with.

What __enter__ hands back

The name after as is bound to the return of __enter__, and to nothing else. Most managers return self, which is why people read as as "the object I opened". It is not that. Return a list and as binds a list.

with Session("run-1") as readings:
    readings.append(3)

Here readings is a plain list, because that is what __enter__ handed back. The session object never gets a name at all. Java scopes the resource to the block and takes the name away at the closing brace. Python does not. readings is an ordinary name and it still works after the block has ended, which is how the last function below returns it.

What __exit__ is told

Three arguments arrive after self.

__exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback)
          |        |          |          |
          |        |          |          where it was raised
          |        |          the exception object itself
          |        the exception class
          the manager

clean exit    ->  None, None, None
block raised  ->  SensorError, SensorError("-1 is below zero"), traceback

So exc_type is None is the entire test for "did the block work". When it is not None, exc_type.__name__ gives you the class name as a string. Their types are type[BaseException] | None, BaseException | None and TracebackType | None. That last name comes from the types module and you have to import it.

The return value, and the trap

Now the part with no Java equivalent, and the heart of this tier. What __exit__ returns decides what happens to the exception.

return True     the exception is thrown away, the caller sees nothing
return False    the exception carries on out to the caller
return None     the exception carries on out to the caller

Truthy and falsey come from the truth and None topic. Return anything truthy and Python swallows the failure. A function that ends without a return hands back None, which is falsey, so the safe behaviour is the default behaviour. You have to type something to break it.

Consider what swallowing costs in a safety-critical system. A reading fails, the manager returns True, the caller carries on as though the sample arrived, and the report says the run passed. The failure is not logged as a failure anywhere, because nothing above the manager ever heard about it. That is the worst defect this course can teach you to write.

So you write it once, here, on purpose. Muffler below swallows, and a test shows you a raise that vanishes without trace. Session does the honest thing beside it. Put them next to each other, watch the difference, and then never reach for the swallowing form again.

Your task

The answer box already holds LOG, a module-level list the tests read, and the supplied SensorError exception. Leave both alone. Every test after the first clears LOG before it starts.

  • Session(name) holds the name and an empty list called readings. On entry it appends f"start {name}" to LOG and hands back that readings list. On exit it appends f"end {name} clean" after a block that finished, or f"end {name} SensorError" after a block that raised, using the exception class name. It lets the exception through.
  • Muffler(name) appends f"start {name}" on entry and hands back itself. On exit it appends f"end {name}", stores the exception's message text in self.swallowed, and swallows the exception. After a clean block self.swallowed stays None.
  • take(name, values) opens a Session(name), appends each value to the list bound by as, and raises SensorError(f"{value} is below zero") on the first value under zero. After the block it returns that list.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Session.__exit__ hands back a falsey value. Work out which values suppress, then never return one by accident.
  • Muffler.__exit__ hands back a truthy value. It is here as the counter-example, not as a pattern to copy.
  • Session.__enter__ hands back the readings list, not the session. A hidden test checks the type.
  • Write no except and no finally inside take. The manager owns the cleanup and the caller owns the catch.
  • Annotate every signature, the three __exit__ parameters included. Import TracebackType from types.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

from types import TracebackType
LOG: list[str] = []
# Supplied. Do not change this exception. class SensorError(Exception): """Raised when a reading cannot be trusted."""
class Session: # TODO: __init__ holds the name and an empty readings list # TODO: __enter__ logs the start and hands back the readings list # TODO: __exit__ logs the outcome and lets the exception through
class Muffler: # TODO: __init__ holds the name and sets self.swallowed to None # TODO: __enter__ logs the start and hands back self # TODO: __exit__ logs the end, stores the message, and swallows
def take(name: str, values: list[int]) -> list[int]: # TODO: one with block over Session(name), append each value, # raise SensorError on the first negative, return the list

testcode.text: print(take("run-1", [3, 7])) print(LOG) LOG.clear() with Session("demo") as readings: readings.append(42) print(readings, type(readings).__name__) print(LOG)

expected.text: [3, 7] ['start run-1', 'end run-1 clean'] [42] list ['start demo', 'end demo clean']

testcode.text: LOG.clear() try: take("run-2", [3, -1, 9]) except SensorError as problem: print("escaped:", problem) print(LOG) LOG.clear() with Muffler("quiet") as muffler: raise SensorError("pressure lost") print("the caller saw nothing") print(muffler.swallowed) print(LOG)

expected.text: escaped: -1 is below zero ['start run-2', 'end run-2 SensorError'] the caller saw nothing pressure lost ['start quiet', 'end quiet']

testcode.text: import inspect probe = Session("probe") assert isinstance(probe.__enter__(), list), "rule broken: Session.__enter__ hands back the readings list" assert probe.__exit__(None, None, None) is not True, "rule broken: Session.__exit__ must not suppress" assert not probe.__exit__(SensorError, SensorError("x"), None), "rule broken: Session.__exit__ hands back a falsey value" assert Muffler("loud").__exit__(SensorError, SensorError("y"), None), "rule broken: Muffler.__exit__ hands back a truthy value" src = inspect.getsource(take) assert "with " in src, "rule broken: take drives the Session through a with statement" assert "finally" not in src, "rule broken: the Session owns the cleanup, so write no finally" assert "except" not in src, "rule broken: let the exception leave take" LOG.clear() print(take("run-3", [])) print(LOG)

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write a transaction manager as a class, write the same behaviour again as a generator, and open several at once with ExitStack.

How this works in Python

Java's try-with-resources calls close() on the way out of the block.

try (Transaction t = new Transaction("run-1")) {
    openValve("inlet");
}

close() cannot see whether the block threw. It gets no exception. So it cannot choose between a commit and a rollback, and it cannot stop the exception either. To roll back you write the catch yourself.

Transaction t = new Transaction("run-1");
try {
    openValve("inlet");
    t.commit();
} catch (RuntimeException e) {
    t.rollback();
    throw e;
}

That try belongs to the caller, and every caller repeats it.

A Python context manager is any object with __enter__ and __exit__. The with statement calls __enter__ on the way in. It calls __exit__ on the way out, however the block ends. Whatever __enter__ returns is what as binds.

with Transaction("run-1") as t:
    open_valve("inlet")

__exit__ takes three arguments after self. On a clean exit all three are None. On a failure they are the exception class, the exception object and the traceback. The manager therefore knows what went wrong and decides what to journal. Java has no equivalent. Their types are type[BaseException] | None, BaseException | None and TracebackType | None, and that last name comes from the types module.

The value __exit__ returns decides what happens to the exception. Return a truthy value and Python swallows the exception. Return a falsey one and the exception carries on to the caller. Truthy and falsey are from the truth and None topic. True is truthy. False and None are falsey. A function that ends without a return gives back None, so the safe case is the default case. Return True by accident and a failed run reports clean.

A safety-critical system that hides a failure has done the worst thing it can do. Work out which value suppresses, and never return it.

You can write the same manager as a generator instead. A generator is a function with a yield in it, from the generators topic. @contextlib.contextmanager turns one into a context manager.

from contextlib import contextmanager


@contextmanager
def transaction(name: str) -> Iterator[str]:
    print("BEGIN")
    try:
        yield name
    finally:
        print("END")

Everything before the single yield is the setup. The yielded value is what as binds. Everything after the yield is the teardown. When the block raises, Python throws that exception back in at the yield. Without try and finally round it, the teardown never runs and the exception walks straight out.

contextlib.ExitStack holds however many managers you turn out to need. Each stack.enter_context(manager) pushes one manager and returns its __enter__ value. Leaving the with unwinds them in reverse order.

Your task

The answer box already holds six things. JOURNAL and ATTEMPTS are module-level lists the tests read. PENDING_FAILURES counts the failures still to come. ValveError is the exception class. retry is your decorator from the decorators topic. open_valve carries @retry(3) and fails the first PENDING_FAILURES times you call it. Leave all six alone.

  • Transaction(name) appends f"BEGIN {name}" on entry and returns itself. On exit it appends f"COMMIT {name}" after a clean block and f"ROLLBACK {name}" after a failure. It sets self.last_exception to None or to the exception class name, and it lets the exception through. One instance must survive being used twice.
  • transaction(name) is the same behaviour written as a generator with @contextmanager. It yields the name and writes the same journal lines.
  • open_many(names) opens one Transaction per name inside a single ExitStack and returns how many it opened.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Return a falsey value from __exit__. Work out which value suppresses, then never return it by accident.
  • Put try and finally round the one yield in the generator version. One yield, no more.
  • Write no try and finally at any call site. Moving it inside the manager is the entire point of the pattern.
  • Do not turn retry into a context manager. Work out why __exit__ cannot run the block again, and write the reason in a comment.
  • Hold no state that a second with on the same instance would trip over. The tests reuse one Transaction.
  • Annotate every signature, __enter__ and __exit__ included. Those three exit parameters have real types, so write them out.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

testcode.text:
run = Transaction("run-1") with run: print(open_valve("inlet")) print(run.last_exception, len(ATTEMPTS))
PENDING_FAILURES = 99 try: with run: open_valve("outlet") except ValveError as exc: print("escaped:", exc) print(run.last_exception) for line in JOURNAL: print(line)

expected.text: inlet open None 3 escaped: outlet stuck ValveError BEGIN run-1 COMMIT run-1 BEGIN run-1 ROLLBACK run-1

testcode.text:
JOURNAL.clear() PENDING_FAILURES = 2 with transaction("gen-1") as name: print(name, open_valve("inlet"))
PENDING_FAILURES = 99 try: with transaction("gen-2"): open_valve("outlet") except ValveError as exc: print("escaped:", exc) for line in JOURNAL: print(line)

expected.text: gen-1 inlet open escaped: outlet stuck BEGIN gen-1 COMMIT gen-1 BEGIN gen-2 ROLLBACK gen-2

testcode.text: JOURNAL.clear() PENDING_FAILURES = 0 print(open_many(["a", "b", "c"])) print(JOURNAL) JOURNAL.clear() try: with ExitStack() as stack: for name in ["x", "y"]: stack.enter_context(transaction(name)) raise ValveError("mid-stack failure") except ValveError as exc: print("escaped:", exc) print(JOURNAL)

expected.text: 3 ['BEGIN a', 'BEGIN b', 'BEGIN c', 'COMMIT c', 'COMMIT b', 'COMMIT a'] escaped: mid-stack failure ['BEGIN x', 'BEGIN y', 'ROLLBACK y', 'ROLLBACK x']

testcode.text:
import inspect
probe = Transaction("probe") assert probe.__exit__(ValveError, ValveError("x"), None) is not True, "rule broken: __exit__ must not suppress" gen_src = inspect.getsource(transaction) assert "finally" in gen_src, "rule broken: wrap the yield in try/finally" assert gen_src.count("yield") == 1, "rule broken: exactly one yield" assert "finally" not in inspect.getsource(open_many), "rule broken: no try/finally at the call site" here = Transaction.__module__ owners = [v for v in list(globals().values()) if isinstance(v, type) and getattr(v, "__module__", "") == here and "__enter__" in vars(v)] assert len(owners) == 1, "rule broken: retry is not a context manager"
JOURNAL.clear() PENDING_FAILURES = 1 with Transaction("probe-1"): print(open_valve("relay")) print(open_many(["p", "q"])) print(JOURNAL)

expected.text: relay open 2 ['BEGIN probe-1', 'COMMIT probe-1', 'BEGIN p', 'BEGIN q', 'COMMIT q', 'COMMIT p']
